title: Museums and young visitors
context: You will hear two arts management students, Hannah and Daniel, comparing how two local museums have tried to attract younger visitors.

lines.t: So, our case study compares how the Riverside Museum and the Castle Gallery have tried to attract younger visitors. Shall we go through the features first, and then do the analysis?
Sure. Let's start with opening hours. The Riverside used to open late on Thursdays, didn't it?
It did, for about a year, but they stopped because the staffing costs were too high. The Castle Gallery still opens late every Friday, until ten.
Right, so that's just the Castle now. What about technology? I read that they both had apps.
The Castle started developing one, but they ran out of money before it was finished. The Riverside's app is really good, though. You scan the labels and hear the curators talking about the objects.
OK. And entry charges. I thought the Castle charged?
It used to, but it's been free since last spring, same as the Riverside, which has never charged anything.
Both of them, then. Now, the Riverside uses students as guides, doesn't it?
That's right, they recruit volunteers from the history department. At the Castle, the guides are all professional staff.
Then there's the exhibition space. The Castle Gallery actually closed two of its rooms, didn't it?
Yes, which surprised me. They said fewer objects, displayed better, would hold people's attention for longer. The Riverside talked about doing the same but decided against it.
And the last feature, letting visitors choose what's on.
That's the Castle. Every year, visitors vote online for the theme of the summer exhibition. The Riverside asks for feedback, but they don't let the public decide anything.
Good. So, why do you think the Riverside has done so well? Visitor numbers among under twenty-fives have doubled in three years.
Everyone says it's their social media, and they are very active online. Or maybe the café, which is really cheap.

The café helps, I'm sure. But lots of museums are active online, and they haven't seen anything like that increase. I think the explanation is much simpler. It's a five minute walk from the main campus.
Hmm, I hadn't thought of it that way, but you're right. The Castle is right out on the edge of town. That has to be the biggest factor.
We'll need numbers to back that up, though. Should we use the figures in the museums' annual reports?
Those are a bit suspect. The Riverside counts everyone who walks through the door, including people who are just using the café or the toilets.
And that newspaper article only interviewed a handful of visitors.
I think our best option is the city council's cultural survey. It asks exactly the same questions about both museums, and it's carried out by an independent company.
Agreed. That's the fairest comparison we've got.
Now, for the recommendations section, I was thinking the Castle should run a free bus from the campus.
That would be expensive, and they've just had budget cuts. What about recommending they finish the app? They've already done half the work.
Maybe, but an app doesn't solve the real issue, which is distance. What if they took part of their collection into the city centre? A small pop-up display in the central library, for example.
Oh, that's clever. It wouldn't cost much, and it brings the gallery to the students instead of the other way round. Let's go with that.
Great. So what's the next step?
I could write to the Castle's education officer and ask whether they've ever considered something like it.
I'd hold off on that until the analysis is done, or we won't know what to ask. Could you track down the council survey first? I'm not sure it's online.
OK, I'll ask at the library tomorrow and see if they've got a copy.
